question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (4y-100)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}y.
$$

Now, we let $u=4y-100.$ Then differentiating with respect to $y$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}y=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $y$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4y-100)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{(1/2)}{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =\frac{2}{4}\cdot {u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4y-100)^{1/2}+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{4y-100}}{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\frac{\sqrt{4y-100}}{2}+C] & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[\sqrt{4y-100}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}[(4y-100)^{1/2}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(C) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(4y-100)^{-1/2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}y}(4y-100)+0 \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4y-100)^{-1/2}\cdot 4 \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{4y-100}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-96-9z)^{-1/2}\,\text{d}z & =\int {u}^{-1/2}\cdot (-\frac{1}{9}\text{d}u) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\frac{1}{(1/2)}{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}{u}^{1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}(-96-9z)^{1/2}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{-96-9z}+C\end{aligned}

$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (-68-z)^{3/4}\,\text{d}z.
$$

Now, we let $u=-68-z.$ Then differentiating with respect to $z$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}z=-\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $z$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-68-z)^{3/4}\,\text{d}z & =-\int u^{3/4}\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{7/4}u^{7/4}+C \\ & =-\frac{4}{7}u^{7/4}+C \\ & =-\frac{4}{7}(-68-z)^{7/4}+C \\ & =-\frac{4}{7}\sqrt[4]{(-68-z)^{7}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}[-\frac{4}{7}(-68-z)^{7/4}+C] & =-\frac{4}{7}\cdot\frac{7}{4}(-68-z)^{3/4}\cdot\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}(-68-z)+0 \\ & =-(-68-z)^{3/4}\cdot(-1) \\ & =\sqrt[4]{(-68-z)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (-13-z)^{3/4}\,\text{d}z.
$$

Now, we let $u=-13-z.$ Then differentiating with respect to $z$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=-1\,⟹\,\text{d}z=-\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $z$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (-13-z)^{3/4}\,\text{d}z & =-\int u^{3/4}\,\text{d}u \\ & =-\frac{1}{7/4}u^{7/4}+C \\ & =-\frac{4}{7}u^{7/4}+C \\ & =-\frac{4}{7}(-13-z)^{7/4}+C \\ & =-\frac{4}{7}\sqrt[4]{(-13-z)^{7}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}[-\frac{4}{7}(-13-z)^{7/4}+C] & =-\frac{4}{7}\cdot\frac{7}{4}(-13-z)^{3/4}\cdot\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}z}(-13-z)+0 \\ & =-(-13-z)^{3/4}\cdot(-1) \\ & =\sqrt[4]{(-13-z)^{3}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
